case: A 41-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-week history of redness, warmth, swelling, and aching pain of her right breast. She is not pregnant or breastfeeding. A 10-day course of oral cephalexin did not help. Her mother died of ovarian cancer at age 49 years. Temperature is 37.0 °C (98.6 °F), pulse is 78/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Examination shows erythema and edema over more than one third of the right breast with peau d'orange and no discrete mass. The breast is warm and tender to palpation. Firm right axillary lymph nodes are palpable. Leukocyte count is 7,200/mm3 (reference 4,500 to 11,000). Skin punch biopsy shows carcinoma cells within dermal lymphatic vessels. The tumor is negative for estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2. The diagnosis is triple-negative inflammatory breast carcinoma.

questions.stem: Before the biopsy, the urgent care physician considered acute mastitis. Which of the following findings in this patient argues most strongly against an infectious cause of her breast changes?
options: Erythema over one third of the breast
Breast pain and tenderness on palpation
Warmth and swelling of the affected breast
approach: List the findings that inflammatory carcinoma and acute mastitis share: redness, warmth, swelling, and pain.
Look for the finding that points to a host response to bacteria.
Acute bacterial mastitis brings fever and leukocytosis; their absence after weeks of a red, swollen breast argues against infection.
questions.why: Inflammatory carcinoma looks inflamed because tumor cells plug the dermal lymphatics, so the breast swells and reddens without any infection. That means there is no fever and no leukocytosis. Acute mastitis is a bacterial infection, usually Staphylococcus aureus in a breastfeeding woman, and it brings fever and a raised white cell count. A red breast in a woman who is not lactating, with no fever and no response to antibiotics, should be biopsied.
whyNot: Both conditions can redden a large part of the breast, so the extent of erythema does not separate them.
Pain and tenderness occur in both mastitis and inflammatory carcinoma.
Correct.
Warmth and swelling are shared features. In carcinoma they come from blocked dermal lymphatics and congestion; in mastitis they come from infection.

questions.stem: Genetic counseling is offered because of her mother's history. Germline testing in this patient is most likely to show a mutation in which of the following genes?
approach: Note two clues: a young woman with breast cancer and a mother with early ovarian cancer.
Breast plus ovarian cancer in a family points to BRCA1 or BRCA2.
The triple-negative, basal-like receptor profile is the pattern typical of BRCA1 tumors.
questions.why: Breast carcinomas are grouped by estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 status. Tumors negative for all three are called triple-negative, and most have a basal-like gene expression pattern. Most breast cancers in BRCA1 carriers are triple-negative, while BRCA2-related tumors are usually estrogen receptor positive like sporadic cancers. A family history of ovarian cancer plus a triple-negative tumor therefore points to BRCA1.
whyNot: Correct.
BRCA2 also raises breast and ovarian cancer risk, but its breast tumors are usually estrogen receptor positive. BRCA2 is the better answer for male breast cancer or prostate cancer in the family.
Germline CDH1 mutation (E-cadherin) causes hereditary diffuse gastric cancer and lobular breast carcinoma, which is usually estrogen receptor positive and not linked to ovarian cancer.
PTEN mutation causes Cowden syndrome, with breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancer and hamartomas. It is not the classic cause of a triple-negative tumor with ovarian cancer in the family.

questions.stem: When she presses her hands firmly on her hips, the right breast becomes fixed against the chest wall, while the left breast stays mobile. Spread of tumor across the retromammary space into which of the following structures best explains this finding?
options: Clavipectoral fascia around the pectoralis minor
Endothoracic fascia inside the rib cage
Superficial fascia just beneath the dermis
Deep fascia over the pectoralis major
approach: Pressing the hands on the hips contracts the pectoralis major.
The breast lies on the pectoralis major from about rib 2 to rib 6, separated from its fascia by the loose retromammary space, which lets the breast glide.
A breast that fixes only when the muscle contracts has tumor attached to the deep pectoral fascia.
questions.why: The breast sits in the superficial fascia over the pectoralis major, roughly from rib 2 to rib 6, with an axillary tail toward the armpit. A loose layer called the retromammary space separates it from the deep pectoral fascia, so a normal breast moves freely over the muscle. When carcinoma crosses this space and invades the pectoral fascia, the breast is pulled tight against the chest wall as the pectoralis major contracts.
whyNot: The clavipectoral fascia lies deep to the pectoralis major around the pectoralis minor. Tumor would have to pass through the pectoralis major first.
Endothoracic fascia lines the inside of the thoracic wall. Tumor there would mean invasion through the ribs and intercostal muscles, causing fixation regardless of muscle contraction.
Involvement of the superficial fascia and the suspensory ligaments that run through it causes skin dimpling and retraction, not fixation to the chest wall.
Correct.

questions.stem: Her reproductive history includes menarche at age 10 years, a first full-term pregnancy at age 22 years, a second at age 25 years, breastfeeding each child for 1 year, and no use of hormonal contraception. Apart from her family history, which of the following elements of her history most increased her risk for breast carcinoma?
options: First full-term pregnancy at age 22 years
Two full-term pregnancies before age 30 years
approach: Recall that longer lifetime exposure of breast epithelium to cyclic estrogen raises breast cancer risk.
Sort each item as adding estrogen exposure or reducing it.
Early menarche adds ovulatory cycles; early pregnancy, more pregnancies, and breastfeeding all lower risk.
questions.why: Breast cancer risk rises with the total number of years the breast is exposed to cyclic estrogen. Early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, a late first pregnancy, and estrogen from fat after menopause all add exposure. A first full-term pregnancy before about age 30 matures the breast epithelium and lowers risk, and breastfeeding lowers it further by suppressing ovulation. Of her history, only the early menarche raised her risk.
whyNot: A first full-term pregnancy at a young age lowers risk because it drives terminal differentiation of breast epithelium. A first pregnancy after about age 30 would raise risk.
Correct.
Breastfeeding suppresses ovulation and lowers breast cancer risk.
Multiple early pregnancies lower risk. Nulliparity would be the risk factor.

case: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of his third episode of dysuria and urinary frequency in 18 months. Two years ago, he was treated for acute bacterial prostatitis. Each later episode has responded to antibiotics, and urine cultures between episodes have been sterile. Between episodes, he has mild perineal discomfort. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F), pulse is 74/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 132/82 mm Hg. Digital rectal examination shows a mildly enlarged, slightly tender prostate with no nodules or bogginess. Urine culture grows more than 100,000 colony-forming units/mL of Escherichia coli with the same antibiotic susceptibility pattern as in the earlier episodes. The diagnosis is chronic bacterial prostatitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would best distinguish this patient's condition from chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome)?
options: Perineal pain lasting longer than 3 months
approach: Name what defines each condition: chronic bacterial prostatitis has bacteria living in the prostate; chronic nonbacterial prostatitis has pain without bacteria.
Ask which test shows bacteria coming from the prostate itself.
A culture of urine taken after prostatic massage, positive when urine before massage is sterile, localizes the infection to the prostate.
questions.why: Chronic bacterial prostatitis means a uropathogen, usually E. coli, persists in the prostatic ducts and reseeds the urine, causing recurrent urinary tract infection with the same organism. Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis, also called chronic pelvic pain syndrome, causes pelvic or perineal pain for months but no bacteria can be grown. Massaging the prostate pushes prostatic fluid into the urethra, so a positive culture after massage proves a bacterial source in the gland.
whyNot: Leukocytes in prostatic secretions show inflammation, which is present in both bacterial prostatitis and the inflammatory form of chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
Mild prostatic tenderness can occur in both chronic conditions and does not prove infection.
Pain lasting months is the defining feature of chronic pelvic pain syndrome and can also occur in chronic bacterial prostatitis.
Correct.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man comes to the physician because of fever, chills, and dysuria that began 1 week after unprotected intercourse with a new partner. Digital rectal examination shows a tender, boggy prostate. Which of the following pairs of organisms is the most likely cause of this younger man's acute prostatitis?
approach: Recognize acute bacterial prostatitis from fever, dysuria, and a tender, boggy prostate.
In older men the usual cause is E. coli or another gram-negative rod rising from the urinary tract.
In younger, sexually active men, sexually transmitted organisms become important causes.
questions.why: Acute bacterial prostatitis presents with fever, chills, dysuria, and a tender, boggy prostate. In older men it is usually caused by E. coli and other gram-negative rods that reach the prostate by reflux of infected urine into the prostatic ducts. In younger men with a new sexual partner, Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae are important causes and should be tested for.
whyNot: Enterococcus and Pseudomonas cause prostatitis mainly after catheterization or urologic instrumentation, not after sexual exposure.
Correct.
Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes are skin and soft tissue pathogens and are uncommon causes of prostatitis. S. aureus prostatic abscess can follow bacteremia.
Tuberculous and fungal prostatitis are rare chronic infections, seen mainly with disseminated disease or immunosuppression.

topics: Causes of acute bacterial prostatitis by age

questions.stem: One year later, after intercourse with a new partner, he has dysuria and a scant clear urethral discharge. Urine culture is sterile. Gram stain of the discharge shows 6 neutrophils per oil-immersion field (reference fewer than 2) and no organisms. Nucleic acid amplification tests for Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Trichomonas vaginalis are negative. Symptoms persist after a 7-day course of doxycycline. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his urethritis?
approach: Neutrophils without gonococci on Gram stain define nongonococcal urethritis.
With chlamydia and trichomonas excluded, think of the other causes of nongonococcal urethritis.
Mycoplasma genitalium has no cell wall, so Gram stain shows no organisms, and it often persists after doxycycline.
questions.why: Nongonococcal urethritis is urethral inflammation without N. gonorrhoeae. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause, followed by Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma urealyticum, and Trichomonas vaginalis. Mycoplasma has no cell wall, so it does not appear on Gram stain and is unaffected by drugs that act on the cell wall, such as penicillins. M. genitalium is also often resistant to doxycycline, so it is the most common cause of urethritis that persists after a doxycycline course.
whyNot: Correct.
Haemophilus ducreyi causes chancroid, a painful genital ulcer with tender inguinal nodes, not urethral discharge.
Gardnerella vaginalis is linked to bacterial vaginosis in women and is not an established cause of urethritis in men.
Treponema pallidum causes the painless chancre of primary syphilis, not urethritis with discharge.

questions.stem: He also reports burning perineal pain that worsens when he sits and eases when he stands. Entrapment of the nerve that supplies the perineum is considered. Which of the following best describes the course of this nerve from the pelvis to the perineum?
options: Out the lesser sciatic foramen, around the ischial tuberosity, and in through the greater sciatic foramen
Out the greater sciatic foramen, over the ischial tuberosity, and in through the obturator canal
Out the greater sciatic foramen, around the ischial spine, and in through the lesser sciatic foramen
Through the obturator canal, around the inferior pubic ramus, and in through the lesser sciatic foramen
approach: Perineal pain that worsens with sitting suggests pudendal nerve irritation.
Recall that the pudendal nerve (S2 to S4) leaves the pelvis, hooks around a bony landmark, and reenters below the pelvic floor.
It exits through the greater sciatic foramen, passes around the ischial spine, and enters the perineum through the lesser sciatic foramen.
questions.why: The pudendal nerve arises from S2 to S4. It leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below the piriformis, curves around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament, and reenters through the lesser sciatic foramen to run in the pudendal canal to the perineum. Entrapment usually happens between the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments near the ischial spine or in the pudendal canal, and sitting presses on these sites.
whyNot: This reverses the nerve's path. The ischial tuberosity is the sitting bone, not the point the nerve curves around.
The obturator canal carries the obturator nerve and vessels to the medial thigh, not the pudendal nerve.
Correct.
The pudendal nerve does not use the obturator canal or wrap around the pubic ramus.

dx: Usual-type (HPV-related) vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia with condylomata acuminata in a woman with HIV
case: A 34-year-old woman with HIV infection comes to the physician because of vulvar itching and growths for 6 months. She stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 15 years. Examination shows multiple soft, exophytic, cauliflower-like papules on the labia majora and perianal skin and a separate 1.5-cm raised, white-gray plaque on the left labium minus. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 160/mm3 (reference 500 to 1,500). Biopsy of a papule shows papillary squamous epithelium with koilocytes. Biopsy of the plaque shows atypical basaloid cells with koilocytic change replacing the full thickness of the epithelium, with no invasion. The diagnosis is condylomata acuminata and usual-type (HPV-related) vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.

questions.stem: Viral typing is performed on the exophytic papules. Which of the following best describes the virus most likely detected?
approach: Soft, cauliflower-like papules with koilocytes are condylomata acuminata, caused by HPV.
HPV is a nonenveloped dsDNA papillomavirus.
Benign genital warts are caused by the low-risk types 6 and 11, while high-risk types 16 and 18 drive dysplasia.
questions.why: Koilocytes, squamous cells with a wrinkled nucleus and a clear halo, are the marker of HPV infection. HPV is a nonenveloped double-stranded DNA virus. Low-risk types 6 and 11 cause about 90 percent of genital warts and rarely cause cancer. High-risk types such as 16 and 18 cause intraepithelial neoplasia and carcinoma of the cervix, vulva, anus, and oropharynx. HSV-2, in contrast, is an enveloped herpesvirus that causes painful vesicles and ulcers and stays latent in sacral sensory ganglia.
whyNot: Correct.
HPV 16 is a high-risk type and the most likely cause of her intraepithelial neoplasia, but benign exophytic warts are usually caused by types 6 and 11.
HSV-2 causes painful grouped vesicles that ulcerate, with multinucleated giant cells, not cauliflower-like warts with koilocytes.
Molluscum contagiosum causes small, firm, umbilicated papules with large cytoplasmic inclusion bodies, not koilocytes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient's HPV infection persisted and progressed to intraepithelial neoplasia?
options: Loss of neutralizing antibody to the L1 capsid protein
Deficiency of terminal complement components C5 to C9
Impaired T-cell clearance of infected keratinocytes
Loss of secretory IgA from the vulvar epithelium
approach: Note the low CD4 count from untreated HIV infection.
Separate preventing infection (neutralizing antibody) from clearing an infection already inside cells (cell-mediated immunity).
Loss of CD4 T-cell help leaves infected keratinocytes uncleared, so HPV persists and lesions progress.
questions.why: HPV lives inside keratinocytes, so once infection is established, antibodies cannot reach it. Most HPV infections and low-grade lesions are cleared within 1 to 2 years by cell-mediated immunity, with CD4 T cells helping cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. In HIV infection with a low CD4 count, this clearance fails, so HPV persists, warts are larger and more numerous, and high-grade dysplasia and cancer are more common. Neutralizing antibody to the L1 capsid, made in response to the vaccine, protects only before infection.
whyNot: Neutralizing antibody to L1 blocks new infection, which is how the vaccine works. It does not clear virus already inside keratinocytes.
Terminal complement deficiency predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections, not persistent HPV.
Correct.
Secretory IgA protects mucosal surfaces against microbes in secretions, but it does not eliminate virus inside infected squamous cells.

questions.stem: Cells from the plaque contain integrated HPV 16 DNA. After exposure to DNA-damaging agents such as tobacco carcinogens, these cells fail to arrest in G1, and immunostaining shows very little p53 protein. Which of the following best explains these findings?
options: Binding of Rb by E7 with release of E2F
Methylation silencing of the p16 promoter
Loss of the mismatch repair protein MLH1
approach: DNA damage normally raises p53, which induces p21 and stops the cell in G1.
Low p53 protein with no G1 arrest means p53 is being removed.
High-risk HPV E6 tags p53 for ubiquitin-mediated degradation by the proteasome.
questions.why: The E6 protein of high-risk HPV binds p53 together with a cellular ubiquitin ligase and sends it to the proteasome. Without p53, DNA damage no longer triggers p21 and G1 arrest or apoptosis, so damaged cells keep dividing and mutations build up. E7 acts at a different point by binding Rb and releasing E2F. Integration of HPV DNA into the host genome usually raises expression of both E6 and E7.
whyNot: E7 binding Rb releases E2F and pushes cells into S phase, but it does not lower p53 protein.
Correct.
p16 is overexpressed, not silenced, in HPV-driven lesions because Rb inactivation removes negative feedback on p16.
MLH1 loss causes microsatellite instability, as in Lynch syndrome. It does not reduce p53 protein.

questions.stem: Which of the following additional findings would best distinguish this patient's vulvar lesion from differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia?
options: Atypia confined to the basal epithelial layer
Background lichen sclerosus in adjacent skin
Large pale cells with mucin-rich cytoplasm
approach: Usual-type vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia is driven by high-risk HPV, in younger women, often smokers or immunosuppressed.
Differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia is not HPV related; it arises in older women with lichen sclerosus and has TP53 mutations.
Strong, diffuse p16 staining marks high-risk HPV activity and so points to the usual type.
questions.why: Usual-type vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia is caused by high-risk HPV, often type 16. It shows full-thickness basaloid or warty atypia with koilocytes, and E7 inactivation of Rb causes strong, block-like p16 staining. Differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia arises in older women with lichen sclerosus, is HPV negative with TP53 mutation, and shows atypia mostly in the basal layer. The two types lead to different kinds of vulvar squamous cell carcinoma.
whyNot: Atypia limited to the basal layer is typical of differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia.
Lichen sclerosus is the usual background for differentiated vulvar intraepithelial neoplasia in older women.
Large pale cells with mucin-rich cytoplasm in the epidermis indicate extramammary Paget disease, an intraepithelial adenocarcinoma.
Correct.

topics: p16 as a marker of high-risk HPV

dx: Dysgerminoma in a 46,XY woman with Swyer syndrome (SRY deletion)
case: A 17-year-old girl is brought to the physician because she has never had a menstrual period and because of 2 months of lower abdominal fullness. She is 170 cm (5 ft 7 in) tall. Breast development is Tanner stage 1, pubic hair is sparse, and the external genitalia are normal female. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a small uterus, a 10-cm solid right adnexal mass, and a thin streak gonad on the left. Serum studies show FSH 92 mIU/mL (follicular phase reference 3 to 12), estradiol below 10 pg/mL (follicular phase reference 30 to 100), LDH 720 U/L (reference 140 to 280), and normal alpha-fetoprotein and hCG. Karyotype is 46,XY with deletion of SRY. Bilateral gonadectomy is performed. The mass is composed of sheets of large clear cells separated by fibrous septa with lymphocytes. The diagnosis is dysgerminoma arising in Swyer syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient's gonads did not develop as testes?
options: Leydig cells were unable to respond to hCG and LH
Bipotential cells were not induced to form Sertoli cells
Primordial germ cells failed to migrate from the yolk sac
Androgen receptors were absent from the gonadal ridge
approach: The early gonad is bipotential in both sexes.
SRY on the Y chromosome turns on SOX9 in supporting cells so they become Sertoli cells, and Sertoli cells organize the testis.
Without SRY, a 46,XY gonad does not become a testis and degenerates to a fibrous streak.
questions.why: SRY is the switch that directs supporting cells of the bipotential gonad to become Sertoli cells. Sertoli cells then build testis cords, recruit Leydig cells, and make anti-Mullerian hormone. With SRY deleted, a 46,XY gonad gets no testis signal and, lacking the two X chromosomes needed to keep ovarian follicles, becomes a streak. With no anti-Mullerian hormone or testosterone, the uterus and female external genitalia develop. The opposite case, SRY translocated onto an X chromosome, produces testes in a 46,XX person.
whyNot: Leydig cell hypoplasia from an LH receptor defect leaves testes present, but they make too little testosterone. Testes still form because SRY is intact.
Correct.
Gonads still form without germ cells. A testis lacking germ cells is a Sertoli-cell-only testis, not a streak.
Androgen receptors are not needed for testis formation. In complete androgen insensitivity, testes form normally.

questions.stem: Ovarian neoplasms are grouped by the cells they arise from. Dysgerminoma belongs to the same histogenetic group as which of the following tumors?
approach: Recall the three main groups of ovarian tumors: surface epithelial, germ cell, and sex cord-stromal.
Dysgerminoma is the ovarian counterpart of seminoma, so it is a germ cell tumor.
Find the option that is also a germ cell tumor.
questions.why: Ovarian tumors are classified by origin. Surface epithelial tumors include serous, mucinous, endometrioid, clear cell, and Brenner tumors. Germ cell tumors include teratoma, dysgerminoma, yolk sac tumor, and choriocarcinoma. Sex cord-stromal tumors include granulosa cell, Sertoli-Leydig cell, fibroma, and thecoma. Dysgerminoma and yolk sac tumor both come from germ cells, and dysgenetic gonads with Y chromosome material carry a high risk of germ cell tumors.
whyNot: Granulosa cell tumor is a sex cord-stromal tumor and often makes estrogen.
Brenner tumor is a surface epithelial tumor with transitional-type epithelium.
Fibroma is a sex cord-stromal tumor of fibroblasts and can occur with ascites and pleural effusion (Meigs syndrome).
Correct.

questions.stem: A buccal smear from this patient is compared with one from a man with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY). Which of the following best describes the number of Barr bodies expected in each?
options: One in this patient and one in the man
One in this patient and none in the man
None in this patient and one in the man
None in this patient and two in the man
approach: A Barr body is an inactivated X chromosome silenced by XIST RNA.
All X chromosomes beyond one are inactivated, so the number of Barr bodies equals the number of X chromosomes minus one.
This patient (46,XY) has one X and no Barr body; the 47,XXY man has two X chromosomes and one Barr body.
questions.why: In each somatic cell, one X chromosome stays active and every extra X is silenced. XIST RNA from the X to be inactivated coats that chromosome and recruits silencing proteins, so it condenses into a Barr body at the nuclear edge. The count depends only on the number of X chromosomes, not on phenotype. A 46,XY woman with Swyer syndrome has no Barr body, and a 47,XXY man has one.
whyNot: This patient has only one X chromosome, so she has no inactive X and no Barr body despite her female phenotype.
This reverses the pattern. Barr body count follows X chromosome number, not phenotypic sex.
Correct.
Two Barr bodies would need three X chromosomes, as in 48,XXXY or 47,XXX.

questions.stem: This patient's labia majora developed from embryonic structures that, in a 46,XY fetus with functioning testes, would have formed which of the following?
approach: Identify the precursor of the labia majora: the labioscrotal swellings.
Recall that dihydrotestosterone makes the labioscrotal swellings fuse in the midline.
Fused labioscrotal swellings form the scrotum.
questions.why: The external genitalia begin the same in both sexes. The genital tubercle forms the glans penis or the clitoris, the urogenital folds form the ventral penile shaft and penile urethra or the labia minora, and the labioscrotal swellings form the scrotum or the labia majora. Dihydrotestosterone from testosterone drives the male pattern. Without testes and androgens, as in this patient, the female pattern develops.
whyNot: Correct.
The glans penis comes from the genital tubercle, which forms the clitoris in a female.
The penile urethra forms when the urogenital folds fuse. In a female these folds form the labia minora.
The ventral penile shaft also comes from the urogenital folds, the precursors of the labia minora.

dx: Periductal mastitis with a subareolar abscess in a smoker
case: A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of a painful lump beneath her left areola. She has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 18 years. She has never been pregnant and is not breastfeeding. She had a similar episode 1 year ago that resolved after incision and drainage. Temperature is 37.6 °C (99.7 °F), pulse is 88/min, respirations are 14/min, and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Examination shows a 2.5-cm tender, fluctuant, erythematous subareolar mass with slight nipple inversion and a small draining opening at the edge of the areola. Ultrasonography shows a subareolar fluid collection. Aspirated pus contains keratinous debris, and culture grows mixed anaerobic bacteria. The diagnosis is recurrent periductal mastitis with a subareolar abscess.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why this patient's abscess recurred after simple incision and drainage?
options: Colonization of the nipple skin by resistant staphylococci
Ongoing milk stasis behind an obstructed duct
Persistent keratinizing squamous lining of the duct
Inspissated lipid secretions retained in dilated ducts
approach: Link smoking, a subareolar abscess, and keratin in the pus to periductal mastitis.
In this disease, lactiferous ducts undergo squamous metaplasia, become plugged with keratin, dilate, and rupture.
Drainage empties the abscess, but the metaplastic duct remains and keeps producing keratin, so the abscess returns unless the duct is excised.
questions.why: Periductal mastitis is strongly linked to smoking. The lining of the lactiferous ducts undergoes keratinizing squamous metaplasia, keratin plugs the duct, and the duct dilates and ruptures. Keratin spilled into the stroma provokes intense inflammation and a painful subareolar abscess, often with secondary anaerobic infection. A sinus tract can open at the edge of the areola. Because the metaplastic duct stays behind after drainage, recurrence is common unless the duct and tract are removed.
whyNot: Resistant staphylococci can cause lactational abscesses, but this abscess grew mixed anaerobes and its cause is the keratinizing duct, not skin colonization.
Milk stasis causes lactational mastitis and galactocele. This patient has never been pregnant and is not breastfeeding.
Correct.
Thick lipid secretions in dilated ducts describe mammary duct ectasia, which usually affects older multiparous women and is not tied to smoking.

questions.stem: Her 67-year-old aunt, who has had five children and has never smoked, has a nontender subareolar mass with thick, gray-green nipple discharge and new nipple retraction. A biopsy is done to exclude carcinoma. Which of the following inflammatory patterns is most likely to be found?
options: Plasma cell-rich infiltrate around dilated ducts
Foreign-body reaction to keratin from metaplastic ducts
Foamy macrophages around necrotic fat with calcium
approach: Note the setting: an older multiparous nonsmoker with a painless subareolar mass and thick discharge.
This is mammary duct ectasia.
Its typical immune response is chronic periductal inflammation with many plasma cells around dilated ducts filled with thick secretions.
questions.why: Mammary duct ectasia affects older, usually multiparous women. Subareolar ducts dilate and fill with thick, lipid-rich secretions that can leak and provoke a chronic periductal infiltrate dominated by plasma cells, which is why it is also called plasma cell mastitis. The later fibrosis can pull the nipple inward, so it can mimic carcinoma and needs a biopsy. Unlike periductal mastitis, it is painless and not linked to smoking.
whyNot: Correct.
A neutrophilic abscess with gram-positive cocci fits acute mastitis from Staphylococcus aureus, usually in a breastfeeding woman with fever and a painful breast.
A reaction to keratin from metaplastic ducts is the pattern of periductal mastitis, which is painful and seen in smokers.
Foamy macrophages around necrotic fat with calcification describe traumatic fat necrosis.

questions.stem: Her 29-year-old sister, who is breastfeeding a 3-week-old infant, develops fever, a cracked nipple, and a red, warm, painful area of the breast that becomes a fluctuant abscess. Which virulence factor of the most likely organism best explains its tendency to form a localized, walled-off abscess?
approach: Lactational mastitis that forms an abscess is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus entering through a nipple fissure.
S. aureus infections tend to stay localized as abscesses.
Coagulase turns fibrinogen into fibrin, which helps build a fibrin barrier around the organisms.
questions.why: Acute mastitis during breastfeeding is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus from the skin or the infant's mouth entering through a cracked nipple. The breast becomes red, warm, and painful, with fever, and an abscess can form. S. aureus is coagulase positive, and coagulase converts fibrinogen to fibrin, which helps wall off the organisms and favors a localized abscess. Group A streptococci, which make streptokinase, tend to spread through tissue instead.
whyNot: Streptokinase is made by Streptococcus pyogenes. It breaks down fibrin and helps infection spread, which is the opposite of walling off.
Hyaluronidase breaks down connective tissue ground substance and favors spread through tissue, not localization.
IgA protease is a virulence factor of Neisseria, Haemophilus influenzae, and Streptococcus pneumoniae for colonizing mucosa. It does not explain abscess walls.
Correct.

questions.stem: At repeat drainage, the abscess cavity is found to extend medially toward the sternum. Brisk bleeding arises from perforating vessels that enter the breast through the second to fourth intercostal spaces next to the sternum. These vessels are branches of which of the following arteries?
approach: Note the location: the medial breast, with vessels coming through the intercostal spaces beside the sternum.
The internal thoracic artery runs down just lateral to the sternum and sends perforating branches through these spaces.
The lateral breast is supplied mainly by the lateral thoracic artery, and the upper breast by the thoracoacromial artery.
questions.why: The breast has three main arterial sources. Medial perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery come through the upper intercostal spaces beside the sternum and supply the medial part of the breast. The lateral thoracic artery supplies the lateral part, and pectoral branches of the thoracoacromial artery reach the upper part. Lymph follows a similar pattern: most drains to axillary nodes, while the medial quadrants also drain to parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels.
whyNot: The lateral thoracic artery runs along the lateral chest wall and supplies the lateral breast, not vessels beside the sternum.
Correct.
The superior epigastric artery continues the internal thoracic artery below the costal margin into the rectus sheath. It does not supply the breast.
The thoracoacromial artery sends pectoral branches to the upper part of the breast from above, not through the parasternal intercostal spaces.
